extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and legislators/educators interested in civic education and political philosophy (readers of Aristotle's Politics)
extracted.subtask_short: music and education in the city
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the role, content, instruments, and styles of musical instruction within civic education — what to teach children, what to forbid, and how to match harmonies/rhythms to moral and social ends. Primarily prescriptive advice for legislators and educators about music's place in forming citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music education must not hinder adult duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The learning of music should never prevent the business of riper years; nor render the body effeminate, and unfit for the business of war or the state; but it should be practised by the young, judged of by the old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulate musical instruction so it occupies appropriate life stages; avoid lifelong training that undermines civic or military fitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children should avoid disputed and virtuosic parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Children should not be employed in those parts of music which are the objects of dispute between the masters in that science; nor should they perform such pieces as are wondered at from the difficulty of their execution, and which, from being first exhibited in the public games, are now become a part of education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach children only material that builds judgment and appreciation rather than technical virtuosity; postpone difficult, contest-style pieces to specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach music to produce proper pleasure and understanding beyond instinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Children should learn so much of music as to be able to receive proper pleasure from excellent music and rhythms; and not that only which music must make all animals feel, and also slaves and boys, but more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for training that cultivates refined aesthetic/moral response rather than mere animal or base emotional reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select instruments suitable for education (avoid highly technical instruments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Children should never be taught to play upon the flute, or any other instrument which requires great skill, as the harp or the like, but on such as will make them good judges of music, or any other instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simpler instruments that cultivate musical judgment; reserve complex, highly-skilled instruments for trained specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flute (and similar instruments) are improper for instructive ends
rubrics_metrics.description: The flute is not a moral instrument, but rather one that will inflame the passions, and is therefore rather to be used when the soul is to be animated than when instruction is intended. The player on the flute is prevented from speaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ban or restrict instruments that inflame passions or impede discourse from the educational curriculum for youth and freemen; permit them where animation (not instruction) is the goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental virtuosity and public-performance training not for freemen
rubrics_metrics.description: Playing like a master (performance to please an audience) should be confined to those who are candidates for the prize in that science or to those who are paid for doing it; therefore we think the practice of it unfit for freemen; for it usually gives people sordid notions, for the end they have in view is bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish civic/educational music from professional entertainment; citizens should not pursue music primarily for public applause or gain—leave that to professionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music has multiple ends; choose harmonies/rhythms by purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody is divided into moral, practical, and that which fills the mind with enthusiasm. Music should not be applied to one purpose only, but many; both for instruction and purifying the soul, and, in the third place, as an agreeable manner of spending the time and a relaxation from the uneasiness of the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the pedagogical aim is instruction, moral purification, or relaxation, and select musical style accordingly; consult specialist treatises for particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use morally appropriate (ethic) melody/harmony in education — favour Doric
rubrics_metrics.description: In education ethic melody and ethic harmony should be used, which is the Doric... the Doric music is most serious, and fittest to inspire courage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise harmonies judged 'moral' (Doric) that foster seriousness and courage in formal civic education rather than ecstatic or merely pleasing forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve Phrygian/enthusiastic forms for animation and certain theatrical/emotional uses
rubrics_metrics.description: The Phrygian music has the same power in harmony as the flute has amongst the instruments; for they are both pathetic and raise the mind... the Phrygian harmony is most suitable to these subjects (violent emotions, bacchanal songs). The dithyrambic measure is Phrygian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow Phrygian and similarly passionate harmonies where the aim is to animate or express violent emotion (e.g., theatrical contexts), but not as the staple of youth instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match musical choices to audience composition and social function
rubrics_metrics.description: Such, therefore, should be the harmony and such the music which those who contend with each other in the theatre should exhibit: but as the audience is composed of two sorts of people... there must be some music and some spectacles to please and soothe them; for as their minds are as it were perverted from their natural habits, so also is there an unnatural harmony, and overcharged music which is accommodated to their taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arranging public performances, balance purifying/natural music with pieces that will soothe or please less-instructed segments of the audience; prefer music 'according to nature' when aiming for universal pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age-appropriateness: consider possibility and decorum (three boundaries)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two things to be taken into consideration, both what is possible and what is proper... but this is to be regulated by different times of life... these therefore are as it were the three boundaries of education, moderation, possibility, and decorum. For instance, the aged naturally suit gentle harmony; the Lydian seems chiefly proper for a child's age as elegant and instructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose musical materials that are both possible for the learner and proper for their age and social role; respect moderation, physical possibility (voice/skill), and decorum in curricular design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music can purify and soothe passions — use sacred music therapeutically
rubrics_metrics.description: We see those persons, by the application of sacred music to soothe their mind, rendered as sedate and composed as if they had employed the art of the physician... all music which has the power of purifying the soul affords a harmless pleasure to man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include musical forms that have therapeutic/moral-purifying effects in education and public performance to restore tranquillity and moderate passions.
